The '''Arctic World Archive''' ('''AWA''') is a facility for [[data preservation]], located in the [[Svalbard]] archipelago on the island of [[Spitsbergen]] of Norway, a mere few hundred metres away from the [[Svalbard Global Seed Vault]]. It contains data of historical and cultural interest from several countries, as well as all of American multinational company [[GitHub]]'s open source repositories, stored on [[silver halide|silver halide film]] stored under the Arctic [[permafrost]] in a large steel vault. It is run as a profit-making business by private company Piqi and the state-owned coal-mining company [[Store Norske Spitsbergen Kulkompani]] (SNSK).

==History==
{{Expand section|date=July 2026}}
Piql is a Norwegian data-storage company that specialises in long-term storage of [[digital media]]. Piql and SNSK created the deeply buried steel vault out of a [[mineshaft]] of an abandoned [[coal mine]]. At the time of its opening as the Arctic World Archive on 27 March 2017, the Brazilian, Mexican and Norwegian governments deposited copies of various historical documents in the vault.<ref name=vincent>{{cite web | last=Vincent | first=James | title=Keep your data safe from the apocalypse in an Arctic mineshaft | website=The Verge | date=4 April 2017 | url=https://www.theverge.com/2017/4/4/15159148/norway-data-vault-svalberd-mine-storage | access-date=13 August 2020 | archive-date=22 December 2019 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191222152606/https://www.theverge.com/2017/4/4/15159148/norway-data-vault-svalberd-mine-storage | url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.nrk.no/viten/xl/dommedagshvelv-apnes-pa-svalbard-1.13439547|title=Dommedagshvelv åpner på Svalbard|last=NRK|date=2017-03-26|access-date=2018-04-16|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180411210030/https://www.nrk.no/viten/xl/dommedagshvelv-apnes-pa-svalbard-1.13439547|archive-date=2018-04-11|url-status=live|lang=no}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.piql.com/arctic-world-archive/|title=Arctic World Archive - Piql|access-date=2018-04-16|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180418225459/https://www.piql.com/arctic-world-archive/|archive-date=2018-04-18|url-status=live}}</ref>

==Description==
The Svalbard [[archipelago]], situated north of mainland [[Norway]], about {{convert|600|mi|order=flip}} from the [[North Pole]],<ref name=nbc/> is declared demilitarised by 42 nations, as established in the [[Svalbard Treaty]] signed after [[World War I]].<ref name=vincent/> This means that the territory cannot be used for military purposes, and the company describes the location as "one of the most geopolitically secure places in the world".<ref name=":0" /><ref name=lindner>{{cite web | last=Linder | first=Courtney | title=Github Code - Storing Code for the Apocalypse | website=Popular Mechanics | date=15 November 2019 | url=https://www.popularmechanics.com/technology/security/a29811351/microsoft-secret-code-vault/ | access-date=13 August 2020 | archive-date=16 March 2021 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210316200734/https://www.popularmechanics.com/technology/security/a29811351/microsoft-secret-code-vault/ | url-status=live }}</ref> The archive facility is on Spitsbergen, the biggest island in Svalbard.<ref name=buried/>
 
The facility is a large steel vault<ref name=buried>{{cite web| title=Buried deep in the ice is the GitHub code vault| first=Nate| last=Byrne| website=ABC News| publisher=Australian Broadcasting Corporation| date=12 August 2020| url=https://www.abc.net.au/news/2020-08-13/github-code-vault-in-artic-svalbard-safeguards-against-calamity/12517948| access-date=13 August 2020| archive-date=6 January 2025| archive-url=https://archive.today/20250106005059/https://www.abc.net.au/news/2020-08-13/github-code-vault-in-artic-svalbard-safeguards-against-calamity/12517948| url-status=live}}</ref> located somewhere between {{convert|150|m}}<ref name=":0"/> and {{convert|300|m}} below the ground or [[permafrost]]<ref name=buried/><ref name=nbc/> inside an abandoned coal mine (Store Norske Gruve 3) that reaches over {{convert|300|m}} into the side of a mountain.<ref name=":0">{{cite web|url=https://edition.cnn.com/2017/04/04/europe/doomsday-library-arctic-trnd/index.html|title=Arctic 'doomsday' vault seeks to protect world's most precious data|first=Paul|last=Lawlor|date=4 April 2017 |publisher=CNN|access-date=2018-04-16|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180418162243/https://edition.cnn.com/2017/04/04/europe/doomsday-library-arctic-trnd/index.html|archive-date=2018-04-18|url-status=live}}</ref><ref name=":1">{{Cite magazine|url=https://www.wired.co.uk/article/norway-data-storage-vault|title=Norway's Doomsday vault will now store and protect the world's data|last=Kobie|first=Nicole|date=2017-04-03|magazine=Wired UK|access-date=2019-11-25|issn=1357-0978|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191108084227/https://www.wired.co.uk/article/norway-data-storage-vault|archive-date=2019-11-08|url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://science.howstuffworks.com/environmental/earth/geology/arctic-world-archive-puts-data-ice-1000-years.htm|title=Arctic World Archive Puts Data on Ice for 1,000 Years|date=2017-04-04|website=HowStuffWorks|language=en|access-date=2019-11-25|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200402134145/https://science.howstuffworks.com/environmental/earth/geology/arctic-world-archive-puts-data-ice-1000-years.htm|archive-date=2020-04-02|url-status=live}}</ref> The facility is secured with a concrete wall and a steel gate. The deposits themselves are stored in secure [[intermodal container|shipping container]]s behind the gate.<ref>{{Cite web|date=2020-08-09|title=Diese Kohlemine soll das digitale Erbe der Menschheit schützen|url=https://1e9.community/t/diese-kohlemine-soll-das-digitale-erbe-der-menschheit-schuetzen/5102|access-date=2020-08-10|website=1E9|language=de|archive-date=18 November 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201118201104/https://1e9.community/t/diese-kohlemine-soll-das-digitale-erbe-der-menschheit-schuetzen/5102|url-status=live}}</ref>

Because of the island's [[Arctic climate]] and resulting permafrost, even if the power to the facility failed, the temperature inside the vault would remain below [[freezing point]], which is cold enough to preserve the vault's contents for decades or more,<ref name=":0" /> with the vault {{convert|250|m}} below the permafrost.<ref name=buried/> The vault is situated deeply enough to avoid damage even from [[nuclear weapon|nuclear]] and [[EMP weapon]]s.<ref name=":1" />

==Long term storage==
Data is stored [[offline]] on film reels made using a refined version of ordinary [[darkroom]] photography technology.<ref name=vincent/><ref name=nbc/> The film is made of [[polyester]] coated in [[silver halide]] crystals<ref name=buried/> and powder-coated with [[iron oxide]], and has a life span of at least 500 and possibly up to 2,000 years, if stored in optimum conditions.<ref name=lindner/>

Realising that people in [[Timeline of the far future|the far future]] may have difficulty understanding what they see in the vault, a kind of "[[Rosetta Stone]]"  has been devised to help decode the data, in the form of a guide to interpreting the archive. The guides are all [[Human-readable medium|readable by eye]], after [[magnification]], and are written in [[English Language|English]], [[Arabic]], [[Spanish language|Spanish]], [[Chinese language|Chinese]], and [[Hindi]].<ref name=buried/>

Clients who pay for the storage of data can send their data digitally or physically. The data can be retrieved at any time from the vault, but it is not a quick process, because the data is not connected to the internet. If data is requested, the relevant reel of film has to be manually retrieved,<ref name=vincent/> then uploaded via a [[fibre optic]] connection to the mainland, to Piql's headquarters in [[Drammen]];<ref name=nbc>{{cite web | title=Look inside the doomsday vault that may hold the world's most important data | website=NBC News | date=7 June 2017 | url=https://www.nbcnews.com/mach/innovation/look-inside-doomsday-vault-may-hold-world-s-most-important-n769341 | access-date=13 August 2020 | archive-date=17 April 2018 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180417122345/https://www.nbcnews.com/mach/innovation/look-inside-doomsday-vault-may-hold-world-s-most-important-n769341 | url-status=live }}</ref> the fastest possible retrieval time is 20–30 minutes, but it can take up to 24 hours with an active subscription and up to 72 hours without an active subscription.<ref name=vincent/><ref>{{Cite web |title=FAQ - Arctic World Archive |url=https://arcticworldarchive.org/faq/ |access-date=2023-04-15 |website=arcticworldarchive.org}}</ref>

===Contents===
The archive stores a wide range of historical and cultural data.<ref name=buried/> Governments, researchers, [[religious institution]]s, media companies and others store some of their most significant records in the vault; Brazil and Norway have archived their [[constitution]]s and other important historical papers.<ref name=nbc/>

The archive includes information about the [[biodiversity]] of Australia, and examples of culturally significant Australian works. It includes the [[Atlas of Living Australia]], and [[machine learning]] models created by [[Geoscience Australia]], which assist in understanding topics such as [[Bushfires in Australia|bushfires]] and [[climate change]].<ref name=buried/>

The archive includes a digitised version of the painting ''[[The Scream]]'' by [[Edvard Munch]] for the [[National Museum of Norway]], and a digitised version of [[Dante]]'s master-work of Italian literature, [[Divine Comedy|''The Divine Comedy'']] for the [[Vatican Library]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.groene.nl/artikel/rembrandt-in-de-permafrost|title=Alles van waarde ligt straks in een oude mijnschacht op Spitsbergen|access-date=2018-04-16|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180418161546/https://www.groene.nl/artikel/rembrandt-in-de-permafrost|archive-date=2018-04-18|url-status=live}}</ref>

In March 2018, German science TV show ''[[Galileo (German TV series)|Galileo]]'' deposited their first show, and made a documentary about it for [[ProSieben]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.prosieben.de/tv/galileo/videos/201875-der-datenbunker-spitzbergen-clip|title=Galileo - Der Datenbunker Spitzbergen|date=2018-03-19|access-date=2018-04-16|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180418162055/https://www.prosieben.de/tv/galileo/videos/201875-der-datenbunker-spitzbergen-clip|archive-date=2018-04-18|url-status=live}}</ref><ref name=galileo>{{cite web | title=German TV program on Piql watched by millions | website=Piql | date=19 April 2018 | url=https://www.piql.com/german-tv-program-on-piql-watched-by-millions/ | access-date=13 August 2020 | archive-date=21 October 2020 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201021055107/https://www.piql.com/german-tv-program-on-piql-watched-by-millions/ | url-status=dead }}</ref>

In October 2020, the first deposit from a [[Nobel Prize]] laureate went to the Archive: 14 books of the 2018 [[Nobel Prize in Literature]] winner, [[Olga Tokarczuk]], were placed on PiqlFilm, undertaken by the Piql Polska and funded by publisher [[Wydawnictwo Literackie]].<ref name="Arctic World Archive">{{cite web | title=Nobel Prize laureate stores life's work in the Arctic World Archive | website=Arctic World Archive | url=https://arcticworldarchive.org/news/articles/nobel-prize-laureate-stores-work-in-the-arctic-world-archive/ | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201024110314/https://arcticworldarchive.org/news/articles/nobel-prize-laureate-stores-work-in-the-arctic-world-archive/ | url-status=dead | archive-date=24 October 2020 | date=9 October 2020 | access-date=11 November 2020 }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last=Sabliński|first=Jędrzej|title=Pamięć absolutna|url=https://www.polityka.pl/tygodnikpolityka/kultura/1977094,1,jedrzej-sablinski-o-tym-czym-jest-swiatowe-archiwum-arktyczne.read|journal=Polityka|volume=45|date=2 November 2020|pages=76–77|lang=pl|archive-date=17 November 2020|access-date=11 November 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201117125040/https://www.polityka.pl/tygodnikpolityka/kultura/1977094,1,jedrzej-sablinski-o-tym-czym-jest-swiatowe-archiwum-arktyczne.read|url-status=live}}</ref>

==GitHub Archive Program==
In November 2019, [[GitHub]] announced that all of its public [[open source code]] would be archived in a code vault at the Arctic World Archive,<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.engadget.com/2019/11/15/github-store-public-open-source-code-arctic-vault/|title=GitHub will store all of its public open source code in an Arctic vault|website=Engadget|language=en|access-date=2019-11-16|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191115221339/https://www.engadget.com/2019/11/15/github-store-public-open-source-code-arctic-vault/|archive-date=2019-11-15|url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.bloomberg.com/news/features/2019-11-13/microsoft-apocalypse-proofs-open-source-code-in-an-arctic-cave|title=Open Source Code Will Survive the Apocalypse in an Arctic Cave|last=Vance|first=Ashley|date=November 13, 2019|work=[[Bloomberg Businessweek]]|access-date=November 17, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191117230310/https://www.bloomberg.com/news/features/2019-11-13/microsoft-apocalypse-proofs-open-source-code-in-an-arctic-cave|archive-date=November 17, 2019|url-status=live}}</ref> as part of its GitHub Archive Program.<ref name=buried/>

In July 2020, the 21-[[terabyte|terabyte]] February site archive was stored at the AWA.<ref>{{Cite web|title=GitHub Has Stored Its Code in an Arctic Vault It Hopes Will Last 1,000 Years|url=https://gizmodo.com/github-has-stored-its-code-in-an-arctic-vault-it-hopes-1844420340|access-date=2020-07-18|website=Gizmodo|date=17 July 2020|archive-date=8 October 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201008022102/https://gizmodo.com/github-has-stored-its-code-in-an-arctic-vault-it-hopes-1844420340|url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|title=GitHub, the world's largest open-source software site, just had mounds of data stored in the permafrost chamber of an old coal mine deep in an Arctic mountain for 1,000 years|url=https://www.msn.com/en-us/news/technology/github-the-worlds-largest-open-source-software-site-just-had-mounds-of-data-stored-in-the-permafrost-chamber-of-an-old-coal-mine-deep-in-an-arctic-mountain-for-1000-years/ar-BB16U75c|access-date=2020-07-18|website=www.msn.com|archive-date=9 October 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201009010534/https://www.msn.com/en-us/news/technology/github-the-worlds-largest-open-source-software-site-just-had-mounds-of-data-stored-in-the-permafrost-chamber-of-an-old-coal-mine-deep-in-an-arctic-mountain-for-1000-years/ar-BB16U75c|url-status=live}}</ref> The data is stored on 186 film reels measuring {{convert|1|km}} long, covered in code stored as [[Barcode#Matrix (2D) barcodes|matrix (2D) barcode]] ([[Boxing barcode]]), which store data very densely (each of the 200 platters of data carry 120 [[gigabyte]]s<ref name=lindner/>). The amount of code stored has been described thus: "If someone who types at about 60 words a minute sat down and tried to fill up all that space, it would take 111,300 years".<ref name=buried/> The first reel holds the code for the  [[Linux]] kernel and  the  [[Android (operating system)|Android operating system]], plus that of 6,000 other major open source applications.<ref name=lindner/>

Further to the general guide to the vault, the "Tech Tree" details [[software development]], [[programming language]]s and other information about [[computer programming]].<ref name=buried/> The Guide and the Tech Tree are written in a collaborative process as a public Git repository.<ref>{{cite web |title=github/archive-program: The GitHub Archive Program & Arctic Code Vault |url=https://github.com/github/archive-program |publisher=GitHub |date=15 October 2020}}</ref>

GitHub's Arctic Cold Vault is a "cold layer" of archiving. The "hot" (accessible [[digital repository|online repositories]]) and "warm" (e.g. [[Internet Archive]]) layers of GitHub's code archives both have the weakness of being founded upon [[electronics]]. It is an incomplete but more secure snapshot of data, with archiving intended at five-year intervals.<ref name=buried/>
